description: Our team consists of members interested in software development, programming, and technology. We focus on creating software-based projects, exploring new technologies, and solving problems through coding. Our work includes research, algorithm design, programming, and testing. We aim to improve our technical skills, gain practical experience, and understand how technology can be used to solve real-world challenges.
summary: APEX-7 is a browser-based, interactive fire-safety dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion findings into something anyone can see, test and understand in seconds. It links two modes. (1) A real-time fire physics simulator of an ISS module: an advection-diffusion model tracks smoke, temperature, carbon monoxide, CO2 and oxygen, so users can switch between Earth (1g) and microgravity (0g) and watch rising plumes turn into slow, oxygen-starved, self-extinguishing flames. Users ignite fires, place and drag six detector types (smoke, heat, CO, CO2, UV, IR), control cabin fans (including the ISS rule of shutting fans on alarm) and get live sensor signals, alarm times and a plain-language explanation of what is happening. (2) A station crisis console where users fight a module fire by extinguishing, sealing hatches, venting to vacuum and rescuing crew, while a smart docking system routes evacuation vehicles. Guided missions teach the core lessons of NASA investigations such as SAME, BASS, FLEX and Saffire: prevention, detection and suppression work differently without gravity. It runs in any browser with no installation, serving students, educators, researchers and designers of spacecraft, Moon/Mars habitats and pressurized rovers.
details:
What is APEX-7?

APEX-7 / ISS Unified Console is an interactive, web-based fire-safety dashboard built for the Flame in Freefall challenge. Instead of asking users to dig through hundreds of PSI combustion records, it lets them experience the core findings of NASA's microgravity combustion research in a live simulation, and then apply them in a station-wide emergency scenario. Live demo: https://apex7-vert.vercel.app/

How it works

1. Detailed Fire Physics mode (ISS module)

  • Physics engine: a 160 × 80 grid (5 cm cells, ~8 m × 4 m module cross-section) solves an advection–diffusion model for five fields: smoke, temperature, carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO₂) and oxygen (O₂), using a semi-Lagrangian advection step plus explicit diffusion.
  • Earth (1g) vs. microgravity (0g): in 1g, hot gases gain buoyant velocity and rise to the ceiling; in 0g buoyancy disappears, so smoke and heat stay around the flame and spread only through ventilation and diffusion.
  • Oxygen-limited flame model: flame intensity grows or decays with the local O₂ concentration around the flame, the flame self-extinguishes when oxygen runs low (~13% O₂), and an oxygen-starved flame produces much more CO. This reproduces the diffusion-limited, self-extinguishing flames observed in ISS experiments such as FLEX and BASS.
  • Cabin ventilation: adjustable fan speed creates circulating flow and a return duct; an optional "automatically shut fans off when the alarm sounds" setting follows the ISS emergency procedure.
  • Six detector types: smoke, heat, CO, CO₂, UV and IR, each with warning/alarm thresholds. Optical sensors (UV/IR) need line of sight and can be blocked by an equipment rack. Users can add, drag and remove detectors and compare detection times, which is the key lesson of SAME/SAME-R: ceiling smoke detectors designed for Earth can be blind in microgravity.
  • Visual layers and tools: smoke, temperature, toxic gas (CO), oxygen and flame-only views; 1×/2×/5× speed and pause; live sensor signal chart with alarm threshold; system event log; and a handheld scanner that measures smoke, temperature, O₂ and CO under the cursor, like the portable instruments used by astronauts.
  • "What is happening now?" panel: a live, plain-language explanation of the physics on screen.

2. Guided missions

  • Mission 1 – Earth vs. Space: Where does the smoke go?
  • Mission 2 – The Fans Stopped!: How detection changes when ventilation is shut down.
  • Mission 3 – Blind Spot: Detector placement, obstacles and optical vs. gas-based detection.
  • Free mode: open-ended experimentation.

3. Crisis & Smart Docking console

  • A station module map with an explosion-triggered fire scenario showing fire intensity, oxygen level, temperature and trapped crew for each module.
  • Per-module actions: Extinguish (limited extinguishers), Lock the hatch, Vent to vacuum to starve the fire of oxygen, and Rescue crew, under an evacuation timer and hull-integrity score.
  • A smart docking/garage system that routes rescue and evacuation vehicles to the nearest free bay, with a dynamic routing log.
  • Linked modes: any module can be opened in the detailed physics simulator, and extinguishing the fire there also reduces the fire on the crisis map.

Why it matters

  • It turns NASA's prevention – detection – suppression framework into intuitive cause and effect that can be understood in minutes.
  • It helps students, educators, researchers and designers reason about detector placement, ventilation strategy, oxygen levels and crew response for spacecraft, space stations, the planned Moon Base, pressurized rovers and future Mars habitats, where oxygen-enriched atmospheres make materials more flammable.
  • It builds on lessons from real incidents (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, the Mir fire) and ISS investigations (SAME, BASS, FLEX, Saffire).
  • Earth benefits: the same principles apply to smoke detection, ventilation control and firefighting in confined spaces such as ships, submarines, tunnels and aircraft.

Tools & technology

HTML5, vanilla JavaScript, Canvas 2D rendering, Web Audio API (alarm and UI sounds), Tailwind CSS, Font Awesome and Google Fonts. It is a single static page with no backend and no installation, hosted on Vercel and runnable on desktop and mobile browsers. The interface is currently in Turkish.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

SI tools were used throughout the project: ideation and brainstorming, researching and summarizing NASA combustion resources, interpreting experiment findings, generating and debugging code, UI and visual design, writing, editing and translation (Turkish ↔ English), and preparing the presentation and demo video. All SI-assisted code and text was reviewed, tested and edited by our team.

Next steps

  • Load PSI dataset records (BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, ACME) for side-by-side comparison and ranking of investigations.
  • A partial-gravity slider (Moon 0.16g, Mars 0.38g) and oxygen-enriched atmosphere presets (e.g., 30% O₂ at 10.2 psi).
  • English localization and a 3D module view.
